common_name: Early Bird Gold Black-Eyed Susan (Day-Neutral Early-Blooming Orange Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; Early Bird Gold (PP20286) was discovered as a sport in a field of Rudbeckia fulgida var. sullivantii 'Goldsturm' at a Louisiana nursery and is day-length neutral, so it begins flowering noticeably earlier in the season than typical black-eyed susans.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Early Bird Gold is a compact, day-length-neutral sport of the classic Goldsturm black-eyed susan, producing the same golden-yellow, dark-coned daisy flowers but starting several weeks earlier in summer and continuing steadily into fall. Its sturdy, upright habit resists the flopping that can affect standard-sized Rudbeckia fulgida cultivars in hot, humid gardens, and the extended bloom window makes it a reliable nectar source for bees and butterflies across a longer stretch of the season. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom, or leave seed heads standing into winter for goldfinches, and ensure good air circulation to minimize powdery mildew in humid climates. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Pot of Gold Black-Eyed Susan (Compact Sullivant's Coneflower)
scientific_name: Rudbeckia fulgida var. sullivantii 'Pot of Gold'

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pot of Gold is a more compact selection of Sullivant's coneflower than the widely grown Goldsturm, staying tidier and lower without sacrificing bloom power.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pot of Gold bears the familiar golden-yellow, dark brown-coned daisy flowers of Sullivant's coneflower on a noticeably more compact, tidy clump than the ubiquitous Goldsturm, making it a good fit for smaller borders and front-of-bed plantings. It flowers from early summer into mid-autumn, drawing bees and butterflies, and tolerates drought well once established even though it prefers consistently moist soil for best performance. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom and keep the display neat, or leave some seed heads through winter for goldfinches. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Crazy Cayenne Threadleaf Coreopsis (Sizzle & Spice Series, Fiery Orange-Red)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Crazy Cayenne is a Sizzle & Spice series threadleaf coreopsis bred for unusually vivid, fiery orange-red flower color on a dense, compact, rounded plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Crazy Cayenne bears fiery sunset-orange flowers with intense red-orange centers and golden-yellow undersides, a striking break from the typical clear-yellow threadleaf coreopsis, held above a dense, compact mound of fine, needle-like foliage. It flowers profusely from early to late summer, drawing bees and other pollinators, and tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil well once established, making it a low-maintenance choice for a sunny border or container planting. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to encourage rebloom and keep the mounded habit tidy. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Whisperin' Yellow Baptisia (Compact Lemon-Yellow False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Whisperin' Yellow is a Growing Wild Nursery hybrid of Baptisia sphaerocarpa 'Screamin' Yellow' and Baptisia alba, combining a compact habit with long flower spikes.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Whisperin' Yellow is a hybrid between Baptisia sphaerocarpa 'Screamin' Yellow' and Baptisia alba, inheriting the compact, floriferous habit of its sphaerocarpa parent along with the long, elegant flower spikes of alba, producing an abundant early to mid-spring display of soft lemon-yellow, pea-like flowers over blue-green, clover-like foliage. It is adaptable to clay, sandy, or average garden soils, tolerates dry conditions well once established, and is deer resistant and essentially maintenance-free, functioning like a small flowering shrub in the border. Dark seedpods follow bloom and provide fall and winter interest; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

common_name: Sunny Morning Baptisia (Butter-Yellow False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Sunny Morning is a Chicago Botanic Garden hybrid of Baptisia sphaerocarpa and Baptisia albescens bearing butter-yellow flowers on gray-tinted stems.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Sunny Morning, a Chicago Botanic Garden hybrid of Baptisia sphaerocarpa and Baptisia albescens, bears soft butter-yellow, pea-like flowers on distinctive gray-tinted stems held above medium to dark green foliage in late spring, producing a fuller, more floriferous display than either wild parent species. It has very good drought tolerance once established and is long-lived and essentially maintenance-free, functioning like a small flowering shrub in the perennial border. Dark seedpods follow the bloom and add fall and winter interest; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut the whole plant back in late winter if a tidier form is desired.
